title: Probability Rules and Conditional Probability
summary: Combining probabilities without double-counting, and the difference between "and", "or", and "given".

lesson.body:
Three operations cover almost everything you will need.

**"Or" — the addition rule.** P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). The subtraction is the important part: without it you count the overlap twice. If the two events cannot both happen — [[mutually-exclusive]] — the overlap is zero and the rule simplifies to plain addition.

**"And" — the multiplication rule.** P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A). Only when the events are [[independent-events|independent]] does this become the familiar P(A) × P(B).

**"Given" — [[conditional-probability]].** P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Read as: among the cases where B happened, how often did A?

The single most expensive mistake in this topic is assuming independence that is not there.

If two bonds each have a 2% chance of defaulting and the defaults were independent, the chance of both is 0.04% — one in 2,500. Reassuring. But if both borrowers depend on the same customer, the same commodity price, or simply the same economy, the joint probability can be a large multiple of that. The individual probabilities have not changed at all; only the assumed relationship between them has.

This is not an abstract concern. Multiplying small probabilities together produces very small numbers very quickly, so an independence assumption is doing enormous work in any calculation of a joint event. **Independence is a claim about the world, not a mathematical convenience** — and in finance it is usually the claim that turns out to be wrong.

A useful discipline: whenever you multiply two probabilities, say out loud what would have to be true for those events to be unrelated. If you cannot construct that story, do not multiply.

lesson.latex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
lesson.plainReading: The probability of A or B is the sum of the two, minus the probability of both — because anything in the overlap was counted once in each term.

variables.meaning: the [[joint-probability]]: both happening. Zero if the events are [[mutually-exclusive]].

lesson.body: Of the deals in a pipeline, 30% face regulatory review (event A) and 40% involve a cross-border element (event B). 12% face both.
walkthrough: **P(A or B)** = 0.30 + 0.40 - 0.12 = **0.58**. Without subtracting the overlap you would get 0.70, overstating it by twelve points.
**P(A|B)** = 0.12 / 0.40 = **0.30**. Among cross-border deals, 30% face regulatory review.
**Are they independent?** Check: P(A) × P(B) = 0.30 × 0.40 = 0.12, which is exactly the observed joint probability. So yes — these two happen to be independent.
The cleaner way to see the same thing: P(A|B) = 0.30 equals P(A) = 0.30. Knowing a deal is cross-border tells you nothing about whether it faces review. **That equality is what independence means.**

Note we *tested* independence rather than assuming it. Had the joint probability been 0.20, the events would be positively related and every calculation treating them as independent would have understated the overlap.

lesson.body:
**P(A|B) and P(B|A) are different numbers**, and swapping them is one of the most common errors in probabilistic reasoning.

Most funds that blew up had high leverage. That does not mean most highly levered funds blow up. The first is P(high leverage | blew up); the second is P(blew up | high leverage). Because there are far more levered funds than blow-ups, the second is far smaller than the first.

This confusion is behind a great deal of bad inference from post-mortems: a list of traits shared by failures tells you what failures looked like, not what predicts failure. Turning one into the other requires knowing the [[base-rate]] — which is the subject of the next topic.

**Diversification is an independence claim.** "Twenty managers, so idiosyncratic risk is diversified away" holds only to the extent their returns are genuinely unrelated. If they are crowded into the same trades, you own one position twenty times over — and the arithmetic of diversification silently stops applying.

**Correlated defaults are the whole story in structured credit.** Tranche valuation depends far more on the assumed correlation between defaults than on any individual default probability. Assuming near-independence across a pool of similar borrowers is the modelling choice that has caused the most damage historically.

**Scenario probabilities need the same care.** "There is a 20% chance rates rise sharply and a 20% chance credit spreads widen" does not make the joint probability 4%. Those two are strongly related, and treating them as separate rolls of a die understates the scenario that actually hurts.

items: "Or" means add and subtract the overlap. Forget the subtraction and you double-count.
"And" means multiply only when the events are independent — otherwise use the conditional form.
Independence is a claim about the world. Test it (P(A|B) = P(A)) rather than assuming it.
P(A|B) is not P(B|A). Most failures being levered does not mean most levered things fail.

questions.stem: P(A) = 0.30, P(B) = 0.40, and P(A and B) = 0.12. What is P(A or B)?
questions.inputHint: Answer as a decimal between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: 0.30 + 0.40 - 0.12 = 0.58. The overlap must be subtracted because it appears in both of the first two terms. Adding without subtracting gives 0.70, which is the classic error.

questions.stem: Using the same figures — P(A) = 0.30, P(B) = 0.40, P(A and B) = 0.12 — what is P(A given B)?
questions.inputHint: Answer as a decimal between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B) = 0.12 / 0.40 = 0.30. Since this equals P(A), the two events are independent: knowing B happened tells you nothing about A.

questions.stem: Which condition means two events are independent?
choices: They cannot both happen at the same time
rationales: That describes mutually exclusive events, which is nearly the opposite — knowing one happened tells you the other definitely did not, which is maximal dependence.
Correct. Independence means conditioning on B changes nothing about A. Equivalently, P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).
Probabilities summing to one describes a set of exhaustive alternatives, which has nothing to do with independence.
A zero joint probability again means mutually exclusive, not independent.
questions.explanation: Independent and mutually exclusive are routinely confused and are close to opposites. Mutually exclusive events are maximally informative about each other; independent events are completely uninformative.

questions.stem: Two bonds each have a 2% probability of default. If the defaults were independent, what is the probability both default? Answer in percent.
questions.explanation: 0.02 x 0.02 = 0.0004, or 0.04% — one in 2,500. The arithmetic is trivial; the assumption is not. If both borrowers share a customer, a commodity exposure or simply an economy, the true joint probability can be many times higher while each individual probability stays at 2%.

questions.stem: "Most hedge funds that have failed were running high leverage. Therefore a highly levered fund is likely to fail." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — this swaps P(levered | failed) for P(failed | levered), and there are far more levered funds than failures
False — leverage has no relationship to failure risk
True — the historical record supports the inference
False — because failure rates cannot be estimated from historical data
rationales: Correct. The evidence is about the composition of failures; the conclusion is about the fate of levered funds. Converting between them needs the base rate, and since levered funds vastly outnumber failures, the second probability is far lower.
Overcorrection. Leverage genuinely does raise failure risk — the flaw is the strength and direction of the inference, not the existence of a relationship.
The record supports the *premise*, not the conclusion. This is precisely the inversion the question is testing.
Failure rates can be estimated from historical data, with the usual caveats. That is not the flaw here.
questions.explanation: This is the inverse conditional fallacy, and post-mortems invite it constantly. A list of traits common to failures describes what failures looked like; it does not tell you the failure rate among things with those traits. That requires the base rate — the next topic.

questions.stem: A fund-of-funds holds twenty managers and argues that idiosyncratic risk is therefore diversified away. What is the load-bearing assumption?
choices: That each manager has positive expected return
That the managers' returns are largely independent of one another
That each manager is allocated an equal weight
That twenty is a large enough sample for the central limit theorem
rationales: Positive expected returns matter for the return, not for whether risk diversifies. You can diversify a portfolio of poor managers just as effectively.

Correct. Diversification benefit comes from returns being unrelated. If the managers hold the same crowded positions, the portfolio behaves like one position held twenty times, and the count is an illusion.
Equal weighting affects the efficiency of diversification but is not what the argument rests on — unequal weights still diversify if the underlying returns are independent.
Invoking the central limit theorem does not help: its conclusions also depend on independence, so this restates the same assumption without naming it.
questions.explanation: Counting managers measures nothing on its own. The diligence question is what they hold and whether it overlaps — which is why crowding analysis matters more to a multi-manager portfolio than the number of line items.

questions.stem: A risk report states a 20% chance of a sharp rate rise and a 20% chance of credit spreads widening, then reports a 4% chance of both. What is the problem?
choices: The joint probability should be 40%, not 4%
Multiplying assumes the two events are independent, and rate shocks and spread widening are strongly related
Nothing — 0.20 x 0.20 = 0.04 is the correct calculation
The individual probabilities are too low to be meaningful
rationales: 40% would be the result of adding them, which is wrong for a joint probability and would exceed either individual probability — impossible for an "and".
Correct. The arithmetic is right for independent events; the events are not independent. Both tend to occur in the same macro conditions, so the true joint probability is well above 4%.
The arithmetic is correct and the assumption behind it is not, which is exactly the kind of error that survives a spreadsheet review.
There is nothing wrong with a 20% estimate. The issue is how the two were combined.
questions.explanation: The scenario that hurts a portfolio is usually the one where several things go wrong together — and that is precisely the scenario an independence assumption prices too cheaply. When you multiply two probabilities, always be able to say why the events would be unrelated.
